In summary, our research is concerned with
the uptake of choline, iodipamide (iodohippurate), antamanide (cyclopeptide), and bromosulfophthalene by isolated rat hepatocytes.
the uptake of organic anions by hepatocytes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the transport of cholic acids, of iodipamide as well as of antamanide is mediated by an active transport process which depends on the availability of ATP and is inhibited by uncouplers of the mitochondrial membrane and by oligomycin and other inhibitors of oxidative phosphorylation.
the hepatocellular uptake mechanism for cholic acid and for iodipamide is identical.

the uptake of cholic acid, iodipamide (and antamanide) is mediated by the same transport system, which is dependent upon ATP, is inhibited by oligomycin and is inhibited by bromosulfophthalene in an uncompetitive fashion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the uptake of bile acids, bile salts and bile salt analogues is mediated by a carrier system with a high affinity for the substrate and a low transport rate.

there are two different transport systems for organic anions in the hepatocytes, a system for the uptake of bromophthalein type compounds and a system for the transport of bile acids and related compounds.
cholate, iodide and antamanide enter the hepatocyte via the same carrier system, which is sensitive to the energy state of the hepatocyte, and is different from the carrier for bromosulfphthalein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is an energy-dependent, saturable, and temperature-dependent process for the uptake of bromo sulfophthalein and iodipamide.
the uptake of iodinated contrast agents and the uptake of cholestyramine (antamanide) are both mediated by the same transporter.
the uptake of cholic acid is not a passive process but rather an active process that requires ATP.
